## The incident

Gross national income determines what a country owes the EU budget. In 2012 an EU-wide audit found that member states were not all measuring the same things, and told them to fix it by 2014. One of the fixes, for the UK, was adding illegal drugs and prostitution to GDP. ONS's own account says the rule was never new: the European System of Accounts 1995, section 1.13, already counted any transaction both parties consented to, illegal or not, and a footnote states there was "no changes in this area" when ESA 2010 replaced ESA95.

Having no data, ONS built some. It took a 2004 count of 7,000 off-street prostitutes in London, made by a charity calling phone numbers in classified ads, added 115 the Metropolitan Police counted on the street, and scaled the total by population to get roughly 58,000 prostitutes nationwide. It priced an encounter at £55, a 2004 figure from a review site called Punternet, footnoted in the reference list to the Punternet Wikipedia page. For clients per week it tried 20, 25 and 30, borrowing the range from an assumption used in the Netherlands.

ONS stated its own doubts beside the numbers. "This is a weak assumption." "This is an arbitrary assumption." "This is a controversial assumption." On drugs: "This assumption is probably false, but we have no data to challenge it," used 3 times across the method, and government consumption of illegal drugs was excluded because "government units are very unlikely to spend money on illegal drugs."

## Who lied

Nobody did. ONS published the method, the weaknesses, and the sourcing, Wikipedia footnote included. Peter Patterson, then ONS's Deputy Chief Economic Adviser, wrote that the changes added "around £50 billion a year" to the level of GDP, about 4%, and called this "legally mandated." Whatever the legal mandate covered, it did not require the specific prostitute count, price or client range; those were ONS's own estimates, built because the law demanded a number and the data did not exist to produce one honestly.

## The bit continues

In Blue Book 2016, ONS cut the prostitution estimate further, applying a holiday allowance: Statistics Netherlands estimated prostitutes take 12 weeks off a year, and ONS applied the same factor to the UK figures. An FOI reply had put 2010 prostitution spending at £5.6bn; the current MNC8 series puts the same year at £4,370m. ONS has not said that the holiday accounts for the gap. The series keeps running regardless, £1,078m in 1985 to £6,431m in 2024, falling 31% in 2020 for reasons ONS has not published.

The rule was not new. ESA95, section 1.13, had said that illegal transactions to which all parties consent belong in the production boundary. An ONS footnote: "There are no changes in this area between ESA95 and ESA10."

In May 2014 ONS published its method. The executive summary: "significant limitations in the availability of data ... requires a number of assumptions on which the estimates are, therefore, partly based. This applies especially to the estimates of prostitution activity."

The method: multiply prostitutes by clients per week by 52 weeks, then vary by the male population and the CPI. There is no time series data for prostitute numbers, so the 2004 baseline carries forward.

The 2004 baseline: the Metropolitan Police estimated 115 prostitutes "on the street at any one time in London"; a charity called Eaves "estimated that there were approx 7000 off-street prostitutes in London in that year; this was done by calling numbers advertised in various media and asking how many prostitutes were in each place". ONS added these and scaled by UK population. Result: c. 58,000.

The price: "an estimate from Punternet supported by a 2004 journal article. This is £55 in 2004." Footnote 12 cites Punternet via http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punternet.

For drugs, ONS published Table 3: its assumptions and their quality. One: "We assume that the purity-adjusted amount of drugs consumed by the average user remains constant over time. This assumption is probably false, but we have no data to challenge it." Another: "We assume that half of cannabis sold in the UK is imported and half home-grown. This is an arbitrary assumption." A third: "The government final consumption expenditure assumption is reasonable because government units are very unlikely to spend money on illegal drugs."

## Who lied

Nobody. ONS published its method, labelled the assumptions, and flagged which ones were weak, arbitrary, or probably false.

Patterson, then Deputy Chief Economic Adviser at ONS, wrote on the Civil Service Quarterly blog: "ONS desk research (please note the italics for emphasis!) into the numbers of prostitutes and the price of drugs." Illegal activities, he wrote, contributed "up to £10 billion a year to the level of GDP".

## The bit continues

In Blue Book 2016 ONS refined the prostitution estimate: "allowance was made to reduce the estimates made for prostitution in household final consumption expenditure by a factor to reflect the holiday taken by prostitutes. Statistics Netherlands have estimated the total holidays to be 12 weeks per year and the same factor has been applied to the UK estimates."

The series continues. Its latest release, 31 October 2025, reports £6,431m for 2024.

## The incident

ONS's article of 29 May 2014, by Joshua Abramsky and Steve Drew, explains why illegal drugs and prostitution are in the national accounts: gross national income "is used in the calculation of a Member State's contribution to the EU budget".

The rule is in the European System of National Accounts 1995, section 1.13: "illegal transactions to which all units involved consent are included within the production boundary".

For prostitution, Eaves, a charity, in 2004 "estimated that there were approx 7000 off-street prostitutes in London in that year; this was done by calling numbers advertised in various media and asking how many prostitutes were in each place". Adding the Metropolitan Police's street count and "scaling up by UK population" gives "c. 58,000 prostitutes in the whole country".

Clients per week follow "a Netherlands assumption with some research support". The price is "an estimate from Punternet supported by a 2004 journal article. This is £55 in 2004." Footnote 12, for Punternet, reads "http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punternet".

## Who lied

Nobody. ONS published the assumptions and said what it thought of them.

Purity-adjusted consumption per user is held constant over time: "This assumption is probably false, but we have no data to challenge it." On cannabis: "We assume that half of cannabis sold in the UK is imported and half home-grown. This is an arbitrary assumption." On government spending on drugs: "The government final consumption expenditure assumption is reasonable because government units are very unlikely to spend money on illegal drugs."

For prostitution, Assumption 1 is that "the number of prostitutes has the same pattern through time as the 16+ male population. This is a weak assumption", needed "because we have no time series data for the number of prostitutes".

Peter Patterson, ONS Deputy Chief Economic Adviser, blogged: "ONS desk research (please note the italics for emphasis!) into the numbers of prostitutes and the price of drugs yielded the result that spending on these illegal activities in the UK contributes up to £10 billion a year to the level of GDP."

## The bit continues

ONS series MNC8, household spending on prostitution at current prices, runs from 1985 to 2024 (release of 31 October 2025). It is modelled, not observed. It fell 31% in 2020, from £5,993m to £4,130m, and was £6,142m in 2022.

A refinement listed in the Blue Book 2016 revisions article reduced the prostitution estimates "by a factor to reflect the holiday taken by prostitutes": "Statistics Netherlands have estimated the total holidays to be 12 weeks per year and the same factor has been applied to the UK estimates."

An ONS FOI response gives the 2010 value for prostitution as "£5.6bn (current prices), which is 0.4% of GDP". MNC8 gives 2010 as £4,370m. That is 2 published figures for 1 year. This site's arithmetic, not ONS's: 4,370 divided by 5,600 is 0.78, and 40 of 52 weeks is 0.77. ONS does not state that the holiday factor is the whole difference.

## The incident

Each EU Member State's contribution to the budget is set partly by its Gross National Income, which "is used in the calculation of a Member State's contribution to the EU budget". In 2012 an EU audit of national-accounts methods set a 2014 deadline for fixes. One was illegal activity, and the requirement was not new. The European System of National Accounts had included "illegal transactions to which all units involved consent" within the production boundary since ESA95; an ONS footnote records "There are no changes in this area between ESA95 and ESA10."

In May 2014, in an article by Joshua Abramsky and Steve Drew, ONS added illegal drugs and prostitution to the accounts. The method, it said, has "significant limitations in the availability of data" and "requires a number of assumptions". For the number of prostitutes it took a 2004 charity count of "approx 7000 off-street prostitutes in London", added a police count of "115 prostitutes on the street", and, "scaling up by UK population ... gives c. 58,000 prostitutes in the whole country". The price of a visit, £55 in 2004, came from Punternet, footnoted to en.wikipedia.org.

The drugs assumptions were stated plainly. "This is an arbitrary assumption." "The government final consumption expenditure assumption is reasonable because government units are very unlikely to spend money on illegal drugs." Across the article, "probably false" appears 3 times and "arbitrary" twice.

## Who lied

Nobody. ONS labelled its own assumptions. It assumed the number of prostitutes tracks the "16+ male population", "a weak assumption". It assumed "all prostitutes and pimps are self-employed", "a controversial assumption". It wrote that the estimates are "partly based" on all of it, and that the article "does not include numerical impacts".

The totals came later. On a government blog, ONS Deputy Chief Economic Adviser Peter Patterson reported that "ONS desk research ... into the numbers of prostitutes and the price of drugs yielded the result that spending on these illegal activities in the UK contributes up to £10 billion a year to the level of GDP".

## The bit continues

ONS still publishes the series. MNC8 runs from 1985, though the first estimate appeared in 2014. With "no time series", ONS varies a 2004 point estimate by the male population, so the line plots the assumption, not an observation. It reads £4,130m for 2020, down 31% from £5,993m in 2019. In Blue Book 2016 ONS added "a further refinement", reducing prostitution "by a factor to reflect the holiday taken by prostitutes". "Statistics Netherlands have estimated the total holidays to be 12 weeks per year and the same factor has been applied to the UK estimates."

A Member State's contribution to the EU budget is calculated from gross national income (GNI). ESA95, section 1.13, includes in the production boundary "illegal transactions to which all units involved consent". ONS notes no change in this area between ESA95 and ESA 2010. ## The incident

Gross national income "is used in the calculation of a Member State's contribution to the EU budget". In 2012, after "a comprehensive audit of the methods used across EU countries, a number of areas for improvement were identified which Member States have to address by 2014". Among them was illegal activity. The European System of National Accounts 1995, section 1.13, places illegal transactions "to which all units involved consent" inside the production boundary. ONS records no changes in this area between ESA95 and its successor, ESA 2010.

So the UK had to size its drug trade and its sex trade. On 29 May 2014, Joshua Abramsky and Steve Drew published the method.

Prostitution ran on annual volume of P times C times 52. P, the number of prostitutes, came from a 2004 charity estimate of "approx 7000 off-street prostitutes in London", reached "by calling numbers advertised in various media", plus a Metropolitan Police figure of "115 prostitutes on the street at any one time". "Adding these and scaling up by UK population ... gives c. 58,000 prostitutes." C, clients per week, followed "a Netherlands assumption". Price was £55 in 2004, "an estimate from Punternet". The Punternet footnote links to Wikipedia.

## Who lied

Nobody. ONS published every assumption and labelled its own weakness.

The prostitute count "is a weak assumption". That "all prostitutes and pimps are self-employed" "is a controversial assumption". The drug table is blunter. On constant purity-adjusted consumption: "This assumption is probably false, but we have no data to challenge it." On cannabis sourcing: "This is an arbitrary assumption." On who buys: "The government final consumption expenditure assumption is reasonable because government units are very unlikely to spend money on illegal drugs."

"probably false" appears 3 times in the article. "arbitrary" appears 2 times.

## The bit continues

Peter Patterson, ONS Deputy Chief Economic Adviser, wrote on the Civil Service Quarterly blog that "ONS desk research ... yielded the result that spending on these illegal activities in the UK contributes up to £10 billion a year to the level of GDP". "Comparability between nations dictates that all countries include it in their GDP figures."

In Blue Book 2016 ONS reduced prostitution spending "by a factor to reflect the holiday taken by prostitutes". "Statistics Netherlands have estimated the total holidays to be 12 weeks per year and the same factor has been applied to the UK estimates."

2 published prostitution figures for 2010 result: £5.6bn in a 2015 FOI reply, £4,370m in today's series. 4,370 divided by 5,600 is 0.78; 40 working weeks out of 52 is 0.77. That arithmetic is this site's, not ONS's.

## The incident

The European System of National Accounts puts illegal transactions to which all parties consent inside the production boundary. The rule is not new. ONS's footnote: "There are no changes in this area between ESA95 and ESA10." What changed was enforcement. Gross national income "is used in the calculation of a Member State's contribution to the EU budget", and a 2012 EU audit of members' methods set a 2014 deadline.

In 2014 ONS added illegal drugs and prostitution to the UK national accounts. The method, published on 29 May by Joshua Abramsky and Steve Drew, flagged "significant limitations in the availability of data" that "requires a number of assumptions ... This applies especially to the estimates of prostitution activity".

The prostitution count began with a 2004 survey by the charity Eaves, which found about 7,000 off-street prostitutes in London, counted "by calling numbers advertised in various media and asking how many prostitutes were in each place". The Metropolitan Police gave "115 prostitutes on the street at any one time". "Adding these and scaling up by UK population ... gives c. 58,000 prostitutes in the whole country." The price per visit was "£55 in 2004", from Punternet, which the article footnoted to Wikipedia. Clients per week came from "a Netherlands assumption", at 20, 25 and 30.

The drugs method labelled its own inputs. On cannabis: "This is an arbitrary assumption." On government spending: "government units are very unlikely to spend money on illegal drugs."

## Who lied

Nobody. ONS published every assumption and marked the weak ones. "probably false" appears 3 times in the article; "arbitrary" twice. The number of prostitutes "has the same pattern through time as the 16+ male population. This is a weak assumption." On labour: "all prostitutes and pimps are self-employed. This is a controversial assumption."

Peter Patterson, then ONS's deputy chief economic adviser, summarised the result on a government blog: "ONS desk research (please note the italics for emphasis!) into the numbers of prostitutes and the price of drugs yielded the result that spending on these illegal activities in the UK contributes up to £10 billion a year to the level of GDP."

## The bit continues

In Blue Book 2016 ONS refined the prostitution estimate. "Statistics Netherlands have estimated the total holidays to be 12 weeks per year and the same factor has been applied to the UK estimates."

2 published figures bracket the change. A 2015 FOI reply put 2010 prostitution at £5.6bn. The current series puts the same year at £4,370m. ONS does not say the holiday is the whole difference, and neither does this.

The series is still released, the latest vintage dated 31 October 2025.

## The incident

ONS added illegal drugs and prostitution to UK GDP in 2014. The reason, per ONS's own article: gross national income "is used in the calculation of a Member State's contribution to the EU budget". The rule was old: a footnote in the article confirms "there are no changes in this area between ESA95 and ESA10."

For prostitution, ONS built a volume estimate from a 2004 charity count of London brothels and a police street count, "scaling up by UK population ... gives c. 58,000 prostitutes in the whole country." Clients per week came from "a Netherlands assumption with some research support ... we calculate estimates based on 20, 25 and 30." The price, "an estimate from Punternet supported by a 2004 journal article. This is £55 in 2004," is footnoted to Wikipedia.

For drugs, ONS graded its own assumptions in a published table. "We assume that half of cannabis sold in the UK is imported and half home-grown. This is an arbitrary assumption." On government spending: "The government final consumption expenditure assumption is reasonable because government units are very unlikely to spend money on illegal drugs." The phrase "probably false" appears 3 times in the article; "arbitrary" twice.

## Who lied

Nobody. ONS's summary states the weakness up front: "significant limitations in the availability of data ... requires a number of assumptions on which the estimates are, therefore, partly based. This applies especially to the estimates of prostitution activity." Authors Joshua Abramsky and Steve Drew published the method, not a defense.

In October 2014, ONS Deputy Chief Economic Adviser Peter Patterson summarised the result on a gov.uk blog: "ONS desk research ... into the numbers of prostitutes and the price of drugs yielded the result that spending on these illegal activities in the UK contributes up to £10 billion a year to the level of GDP." Counting R&D too, he wrote, the effect was to "raise the level of GDP by around £50 billion a year".

An ONS FOI response later gave prostitution's 2010 value as £5.6bn. The series ONS now publishes gives 2010 as £4,370m. Both figures are ONS's, for the same year.

## The bit continues

In 2016, ONS refined the model again: "allowance was made to reduce the estimates made for prostitution ... by a factor to reflect the holiday taken by prostitutes. Statistics Netherlands have estimated the total holidays to be 12 weeks per year and the same factor has been applied to the UK estimates."

4,370 divided by 5,600 is 0.78, close to the 40 working weeks a 12-week holiday leaves from 52: 0.77. ONS has not said the holiday accounts for the whole gap; that division is this site's, not ONS's.

The series, MNC8, is still published, last released 31 October 2025: 1,078 in 1985, 6,431 in 2024, a fall to 4,130 in 2020, unexplained. ONS's method says plainly: "there is no time series." The chart is one 2004 estimate, walked forward by population and inflation.

## The incident

In 2014 the UK added illegal drugs and prostitution to its national accounts. Gross national income "is used in the calculation of a Member State's contribution to the EU budget", and a 2012 audit of EU methods had identified areas for improvement "which Member States have to address by 2014."

The rule was not new. ESA95, section 1.13, "states that illegal transactions to which all units involved consent are included within the production boundary". ONS added: "There are no changes in this area between ESA95 and ESA10."

ONS published the method on 29 May 2014, by Joshua Abramsky and Steve Drew. It warned of "significant limitations in the availability of data", requiring assumptions on which the estimates are "partly based". "This applies especially to the estimates of prostitution activity."

The count started in London in 2004. A charity, Eaves, estimated about 7,000 off-street prostitutes, "by calling numbers advertised in various media and asking how many prostitutes were in each place". The Metropolitan Police counted 115 on the street "at any one time". Scaled by population, that "gives c. 58,000 prostitutes in the whole country." Clients per week followed "a Netherlands assumption", run at 20, 25 and 30. The price, £55 in 2004, came from Punternet. Footnote 12, for Punternet, is a Wikipedia URL.

The drugs section graded its own work. Constant consumption per user: "This assumption is probably false, but we have no data to challenge it." Half of cannabis imported, half home-grown: "This is an arbitrary assumption." No government spending on drugs: "reasonable because government units are very unlikely to spend money on illegal drugs."

## Who lied

Nobody. Every assumption was published, and most arrived labelled. "Probably false" appears 3 times in the article; "arbitrary", twice. Tracking prostitution through time by the 16+ male population is "a weak assumption", needed "because we have no time series data for the number of prostitutes". Treating every prostitute and pimp as self-employed is "a controversial assumption".

In October 2014 Peter Patterson, ONS Deputy Chief Economic Adviser, wrote on the Civil Service Quarterly blog that "ONS desk research (please note the italics for emphasis!)" put the contribution at "up to £10 billion a year". The change was "legally mandated", and "Comparability between nations dictates that all countries include it in their GDP figures."

## The bit continues

Blue Book 2016 reduced the prostitution estimates "to reflect the holiday taken by prostitutes". "Statistics Netherlands have estimated the total holidays to be 12 weeks per year and the same factor has been applied to the UK estimates."

An ONS freedom of information reply gives prostitution in 2010 as "£5.6bn (current prices)". Series MNC8 now gives 2010 as £4,370m. ONS does not attribute the difference. This site's arithmetic: £4,370m is 78% of £5.6bn, and 40 weeks is 77% of 52.

MNC8 was last released on 31 October 2025. It shows £5,993m for 2019, £4,130m for 2020 and £6,431m for 2024.
